attachment_r_sources.heading: Generating RTS units
attachment_r_sources.title: Generating Real-Time Strategy Game Units Using Search-Based Procedural Content Generation and Monte Carlo Tree Search.
attachment_r_sources.original_bibliographic_paragraph: Kynan Sorochan and Matthew Guzdial. **Generating Real-Time Strategy Game Units Using Search-Based Procedural Content Generation and Monte Carlo Tree Search.** Experimental AI in Games Workshop, 2022. [arXiv:2212.03387v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.03387v1). Inspected: Search Space, Evaluator, Search Method, generated units, evaluation and references.
attachment_r_sources.bibliographic_verification: Verified for arXiv title/authors/identifier; workshop metadata retained from the supplied record.
attachment_r_sources.inherited_access: Inspected: Search Space, Evaluator, Search Method, generated units, evaluation and references.
attachment_r_sources.relevance: Explicit triggers/effects and tests of new-unit contribution.
attachment_r_sources.limitations: Predefined search vocabulary, one-map/evaluator limitations; no character-to-mechanics learning.
reported_observations: The system adds a fourth military unit to microRTS. It searches numerical attributes and a human-authored vocabulary of four causes and four effects. Causes include taking damage and dealing damage; effects include resource return, additional attacks, healing and attack-speed changes. Greedy search changes attributes or cause/effect choices. Each candidate evaluation uses 20 games: ten with asymmetric access to the new unit and ten with access for both sides. Later evaluation compares agents with different search budgets. Ten generated units are presented.

Limits: this is invention within a supplied vocabulary. Its utility measure includes unit lifetime, which may undervalue disposable or burst units. Symmetric win rates cannot by themselves rule out a mandatory purchase or a collapsed strategy space. Those are our criticisms of transferring the evaluator, not additional results reported by the authors. Tower defense also lacks the same adversarial purchase structure. Incoming damage, death and movement must not be imported into a Definition that does not support them.

Additional limitation from the expanded reading: the evaluation uses one map, and the strongest agent often underuses the new units. Its preference for the original roster can confound unit usefulness with evaluator competence. The search budgets are not validated human skill models; generated names and shared visuals are not evidence of visual-content generation.

attachment_r_sources.inherited_access: Inspected: quality measurements, human comparisons, Experiment III and conclusions. The filename is not the publication year.
attachment_r_sources.relevance: Paired human preferences and simulation-derived quality in formal games.
attachment_r_sources.limitations: Preference prediction is game-family and sample dependent; no universal taste or historical-originality certificate.
reported_observations: Ludi evolves formal game rules and uses self-play features to estimate human preferences. The paper reports 1,389 evolved games, 19 deemed viable, and 127 paired comparisons of those viable games from 27 participants in the follow-up study. Yavalath and Ndengrod were commercially published. Ndengrod independently rediscovered Irensei on a different grid; the authors describe Yavalath's four-in-a-row win combined with an earlier three-in-a-row loss as an unpublished rule combination.

Limits: preference prediction is specific to the sample and game family. Generating a viable game, predicting a preference and proving historical originality are different achievements. Its learned coefficients are not tower defense quality weights. Do not treat 19 viable games as 19 independently established historical inventions.

attachment_r_sources.heading: GAVEL
attachment_r_sources.title: GAVEL: Generating Games Via Evolution and Language Models.
attachment_r_sources.original_bibliographic_paragraph: Graham Todd, Alexander G. Padula, Matthew Stephenson, Éric Piette, Dennis J. N. J. Soemers and Julian Togelius. **GAVEL: Generating Games Via Evolution and Language Models.** NeurIPS 2024. [arXiv:2407.09388v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.09388v2). Inspected: representation, mutation, evaluation, experiments, results, limitations and references. [Code link](https://github.com/gdrtodd/gavel), not executed in this investigation.
attachment_r_sources.bibliographic_verification: Verified for arXiv record; supplied NeurIPS attribution retained.
attachment_r_sources.inherited_access: Inspected: representation, mutation, evaluation, experiments, results, limitations and references. [Code link](https://github.com/gdrtodd/gavel), not executed in this investigation.
attachment_r_sources.relevance: Executable rule mutation, staged evaluation and retention of alternatives.
attachment_r_sources.limitations: Board-game metrics, expensive search, unused components and inconclusive novelty-cell improvement do not establish TD taste.
reported_observations: GAVEL combines a code language model, Ludii game descriptions and quality-diversity search. It mutates portions of executable rules and evaluates candidates through staged checks and simulated games. Evaluation includes balance, decisiveness, completion, agency, board coverage and a strategic-depth proxy. It retains high-fitness representatives in a concept-based archive.

The paper reports significant improvements over its baselines in QD score and archive coverage, but improvements in novel occupied cells were not statistically significant over three runs. Preliminary expert playtesting found promising examples, including Yavalath-derived line conditions combined with Go-style enclosure capture. Each search run took roughly 48 hours using an RTX8000 GPU and parallel evaluation on 16 CPU cores with 128 GB memory. This is not evidence of interactive latency.

A particularly relevant failure is unused components: adding dice to equipment need not make dice affect gameplay. Our equivalent could be an upgrade with no reachable trigger or an attack-origin feature that never changes delivery. Static checks can detect some unreachable or redundant definitions; actual use requires runtime evidence. The authors also note that temporarily unused components can be useful intermediate search states. Keep such drafts out of accepted output without erasing their research value.

Stanley. **Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone.** Evolutionary Computation 19(2), pages 189 to 223, 2011. [Primary-text PDF](https://www.cs.swarthmore.edu/~meeden/DevelopmentalRobotics/lehman_ecj11.pdf). Inspected: motivation, behavioral novelty, experimental tasks and discussion. attachment_r_sources.relevance: Avoid prematurely removing unusual behavior solely for one objective.

reported_observations: Novelty search rewards behavioral difference rather than progress toward a fixed objective. The experiments show benefits in deceptive maze-navigation and biped-walking tasks. Limits: novelty is neither usefulness nor fit. Our output still needs supported mechanics and project constraints. This paper is a reason to inspect the effects of our ranking criteria, not a reason to remove quality checks.

attachment_r_sources.heading: Restricted-play evaluation
attachment_r_sources.title: Evaluating Competitive Game Balance with Restricted Play.
attachment_r_sources.original_bibliographic_paragraph: Alexander Jaffe, Alex Miller, Erik Andersen, Yun-En Liu, Anna Karlin and Zoran Popović. **Evaluating Competitive Game Balance with Restricted Play.** AIIDE 2012. [Author-hosted PDF](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~zoran/jaffe2012ecg.pdf). Inspected: framework, example application and conclusions. Reached through R1 → R7 → R8.
attachment_r_sources.bibliographic_verification: Title/authors verified in author PDF; venue retained from attachment.
attachment_r_sources.inherited_access: Inspected: framework, example application and conclusions. Reached through R1 → R7 → R8.
attachment_r_sources.relevance: Compare access to a mechanic and rule removal under controlled conditions.
attachment_r_sources.limitations: Weak agents, scenario choice and policy adaptation can confound usefulness.
reported_observations: The framework turns balance questions into comparisons between standard agents and agents with carefully restricted options. Its application to an educational card game demonstrates a way to investigate the value of game elements through controlled restrictions.

Distinguish two experiments. Restricting an agent's choices asks whether access to an option matters. Removing a mechanic from the rules asks how that mechanic changes the game. Both can be useful, but they need not produce the same answer. Allow policies to adapt to each condition; otherwise a policy trained for the original rules can make the alternative look artificially weak.

Limits: no observed difference can mean irrelevance, weak agents, unsuitable scenarios or insufficient trials. A large difference can indicate excessive power rather than good design. Pair outcome measurements with changed decisions and retained weaknesses.
